problem: Existing robot learning platforms either have simple, context-free scenes (IsaacGym/IsaacLab) or low training throughput without GPU parallelization (CARLA, MetaDrive), so they cannot support large-scale, diverse, interactive training for urban micromobility. Existing AI solutions also target isolated skills (obstacle avoidance, parkour) rather than the versatile skills micromobility needs.
motivation: Micromobility devices such as delivery robots and mobility scooters operate on sidewalks and plazas with varied terrain and dense pedestrians. Human operation is unsafe and labor-intensive, so autonomous agents are needed, and these need to be trained on abundant diverse scenes at high throughput. The paper observes that 'large-scale' and 'high-performance' training conflict on current platforms, and resolves this with asynchronous sampling of non-uniform scenes on the GPU.
key_idea: Build a GPU-parallel urban simulator (URBAN-SIM) that procedurally generates diverse interactive scenes and samples different scenes asynchronously per environment, plus a benchmark (URBAN-BENCH) of 8 tasks covering locomotion, navigation and kilometer-scale traverse across four robot embodiments.
insight: Scene diversity in parallel training matters a lot: on NavStatic, going from 1 to 1,024 training scenes raises Success Rate from 5.1% to 83.2%, and asynchronous sampling (a unique scene per environment) increasingly outperforms IsaacLab-style synchronous sampling (identical scenes) as scenes go from 8 to 256. Each embodiment has distinct strengths (quadruped for smoothness/safety, wheeled-legged for locomotion range, humanoid for cluttered navigation). The appendix ablation shows that terrain-specific locomotion experts beat a general mixed-terrain policy, and that navigation performance declines roughly linearly as training area grows, which motivates composing small foundational skills for long-horizon traverse.
method: Hierarchical Urban Generation: four-stage procedural pipeline of block connection, ground planning into functional zones, terrain generation via Wave Function Collapse (flat/stair/slope/rough) and object placement from 15,000+ 3D assets, giving unbounded scenes from 25 m² up to 200,000 m².

Interactive Dynamics Generation: ORCA multi-agent path planning reimplemented in JAX so pedestrians, cyclists and vehicles run on GPU and react to the trained robot in real time, using a 2D occupancy map with random start/end points.

Asynchronous Scene Sampling: assets are cached and each parallel environment randomly samples assets to build a unique scene, with observations, rewards and actions vectorized on GPU; about 1,800-2,600 fps with RGBD on one L40S at 256 envs.

URBAN-BENCH tasks: 4 locomotion tasks (LocoFlat/Slope/Stair/Rough), 3 navigation tasks (NavClear/Static/Dynamic) and 1 kilometer-scale Traverse task, evaluated on wheeled COCO, Unitree Go2, B2-W and G1 robots.

Policies: PPO-trained locomotion (elevation map, proprioception, velocity commands → joint targets) and navigation (RGBD, position and goal → 2D velocity command) per terrain/scenario, giving a 24-model matrix.

Human-AI shared autonomy for Traverse: three-layer control (high-level decision, mid-level navigation, low-level locomotion), where humans at decision points either take over or dispatch nav/loc expert policies; four modes (Human, Human-AI-Mode-1, Human-AI-Mode-2, AI).

setting.backbone: PPO-trained RL policies (per-robot, per-task) trained from scratch; no pretrained models
setting.training_data: Procedurally generated simulation scenes: 768 Urban-Nav training scenes (256x3, 10m x 10m) and Urban-Loc terrain grids (30x30 regions with curriculum); 8/18/24 h on one L40S for NavClear/Static/Dynamic
setting.observation: Navigation: 128x128 RGB-D, position/goal vector, projected velocity, 1.6 m x 1.0 m height map; locomotion: proprioception, velocities, height map
setting.action_space: Navigation: 2D normalized velocity command (x, y) passed to a locomotion policy or Ackermann model; locomotion: low-level joint targets/wheel velocities (12/16/37 joints for Go2/G1/B2W)
setting.privileged: none (Traverse uses human operators at decision points; scene routes were manually set)

numbers.extra: 15m x 15m test regions with the same textures as training

numbers.method: PPO nav policy trained on 1,024 scenes vs 1 scene
numbers.extra: Scaling study; SR from 1 to 1,024 training scenes
numbers.evidence: Rising from 5.1% to 83.2% (Success Rate) as training scenes increase from 1 to 1,024

numbers.extra: Human at decision points; 1,200 m route

numbers_note: Locomotion table (Balance, X-displacement, TTF, Smoothness for three robots) is not itemized here; asynchronous vs synchronous sampling results and the foundational-task ablation are figures only. Only main rows for a subset of robots are listed; the Human and Human-AI-Mode-2 traverse rows are also in the appendix table.
results: URBAN-SIM reaches 1,800-2,600 fps with 256 parallel environments on a single L40S. On URBAN-BENCH, the wheeled robot is best on NavClear (SR 97.6%), while the humanoid leads on NavStatic and NavDynamic (SR 77.86% / 79.23%) and the quadruped has the lowest collisions (0.08 / 0.13). In Traverse, full Human control gives the best completeness and safety (4 trials, 15 collisions) but the highest labor cost (1189.27 s), full AI has zero labor but 66 trials and 49 collisions, and shared modes fall in between.
limitations: No real-world experiments in the paper: sim-to-real is only mentioned as preliminary and future work (ROS2 pipeline planned).

Procedurally generated scenes do not fully match real-world data distributions (e.g., no OpenStreetMap-based digital twins), and capabilities such as manipulation and multi-modal perception are absent.
The benchmark uses plain PPO baselines with no strong navigation methods, and Traverse relies on manual human dispatch and hand-tuned routes evaluated on a single quadruped.
